newsitem.title: PERU: Negotiated solution to Peru siege looks possible.
newsitem.headline: Negotiated solution to Peru siege looks possible.

text.p: A peaceful end to Peru's 12-day-old hostage crisis looked more possible on Sunday after the government and Marxist rebels holding 83 VIP captives softened their "no compromise" positions and met face-to-face for the first time.

President Alberto Fujimori sent his mediator, Education Minister Domingo Palermo, for a long meeting on Saturday with rebel leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini inside the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence.
The result of that meeting was immediate: the release of 20 hostages, leaving 83 behind.

With the exception of several 1993 meetings that Fujimori had with Abimael Guzman, the imprisoned leader of the Shining Path guerrilla movement, no government official has held direct talks with Peruvian insurgents in 16 years of conflict.
In a statement read by one of the newly freed captives, the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas expressed a willingness "to withdraw from the occupied residence by way of dialogue."
The communique, which struck a more conciliatory tone than two previous statements, made no mention of their main condition -- the release of around 400 imprisoned comrades.
The rebels had initially threatened to kill their hostages if their colleagues were not freed. As of Sunday, they had released more than 420 of the original captives unharmed.

Backing up the new mood, the MRTA's international spokesman, Isaac Velazco, told Reuters on Sunday the rebels were prepared to negotiate their original demand and could settle for an "intermediate solution."

"We still insist on the liberation of the political prisoners, but we consider that an intermediate solution can be reached," he said in an interview from Hamburg. Asked what that meant, he said: "Not necessarily the liberation of all the political prisoners."
He added that the release of the 20 hostages on Saturday by the rebels was a gesture of flexibility in response to the government's first face-to-face meeting with the MRTA.

Palermo said following the release of the 20 hostages -- mostly Peruvian diplomats and Japanese businessmen -- that there had been "advances for the solution of this serious incident," but gave no details.
The moves brought fresh hope in Peru, where the population is weary of guerrilla violence and embarrassed by the international attention caused by the current crisis.
"The danger of a violent way out is growing more distant," the anti-government daily La Republica said on its front page on Sunday.
Columnist Jaime De Althaus wrote in the daily Expreso that the first direct talks represented "a gigantic step forward, which raises the prospect of a way out."
In Tokyo, Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto welcomed the new moves but warned against an overly optimistic view.

"It is not time yet to get our hopes up but reading the guerrillas' demands, it seems possible to have a dialogue with the rebels," he told reporters. He said the remaining hostages were still facing a "tough situation".

In a letter to Hashimoto carried out by nine freed Japanese hostages released on Saturday, the remaining Japanese captives -- about 20 diplomats and businessmen -- warned that their plight was becoming more dangerous.

"If the situation in which heavily armed soldiers keep a close watch on us lasts for a long time, it will become extremely difficult for us to keep the balance between mind and body," the letter said.
Hashimoto said he planned to contact Fujimori, himself the son of Japanese immigrants to Peru, to see if negotiations could be speeded up.
The latest testimonies from released hostages and Red Cross officials indicated that the atmosphere inside the residence was calm and that there were no serious health problems.
Dominican Republic Ambassador Jose Diaz, among those released on Saturday, said spirits were high.

"We all received a respectful treatment (from the rebels). Everyone is and was in high sprits, waiting for a solution," he told reporters. "To those who are inside, I tell them to have faith in God, we all hope that things are resolved peacefully."

Diaz singled out for praise Peruvian Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela -- the guerrillas' most high-profile hostage. "He has shown an important attitude. Before going, I congratulated him and I felt comforted when I saw his courage. All Peruvians should be proud of their foreign minister."

The International Red Cross welcomed the direct talks as a major step forward in the crisis, but warned that an early solution was not guaranteed. "The fact that members of the guerrilla group and representatives of the government met does not mean the problem is simple ... It means that discussions are starting and disagreement is still there," Red Cross chief representative Michel Minnig said in a television interview.
